b: GM Javokhir Sindarov will start the 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship with the white pieces in Geneva on Tuesday after World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju selected a clock containing a black knight at the opening ceremony. Earlier, at the press conference, Sindarov noted how short his six months of preparation had seemed, while Gukesh, asked about defending his title, commented, "I don’t think I’m here to defend anything—I’m here to win it all over again!"

For the players, the key detail of the media day before the match is getting to know who will make the first move. That was decided in the opening ceremony that took place Sunday in the impressive Palace of Nations. In Singapore in 2024, the colors for the first game of GM Ding Liren's match against Gukesh were decided in a dramatic laser display. This time, it was done in more understated Swiss style as Gukesh got to select from a pair of clocks—containing light or dark chocolate knights.

The moment @DGukesh picked a clock with a black chocolate knight inside and therefore starts with Black vs. @GMJSindarov in Tuesday's Game 1 of the 2026 FIDE World Championship! #GukeshSindarov https://t.co/57JyfsNY5z

Sindarov will now have the white pieces and make the first move in game one on Tuesday—the game starts 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST, and we'll have commentary from GMs Judit Polgar and David Howell—before Gukesh and Sindarov alternate colors for the remaining 13 games. The first rest day is on Friday, after three games have been played.
Sindarov was left with the white knight, meaning he gets White in game one. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.
You can watch the full opening ceremony below.

The match itself will take place in the Fondation Martin Bodmer, a library and museum in Cologny, overlooking Lake Geneva, but the opening press conference was also held at the United Nations building, in the Kazakh room, hence the presence of the Kazakh ambassador as well as host GM Maurice Ashley and FIDE President Timur Turlov.
The opening press conference is a long-standing tradition. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.
The players spent almost an hour talking about the match, and again, you can watch that below.
If you'd prefer to read, we've transcribed all the players' answers below:
How different is playing the World Championship as the reigning champion?

Gukesh: First of all, I’m really glad to be here, glad to be in Geneva for this match. I think compared to the last time it feels like I’m more experienced coming into the match, but whatever has happened till now just gets erased when we sit at the table for game one. It’s a completely different match, a completely different opponent, a different place, so I’m not really thinking about other things, just giving my best for these 14 games.
Whatever has happened till now just gets erased when we sit at the table for game one.

I think Sindarov has just been in very consistent and very good form, and surely one of the very top players at the very top of his game, so it’s for sure going to be a real test, but I have prepared the best way that I can and I’m very enthusiastic for this match—to test myself against such a strong player and to see what I’m capable of.
How has the last six months since winning the Candidates been?

Sindarov: After Cyprus, I played a lot of tournaments in a row, and this six months, I was thinking I have a lot of time, but it passed very fast, I was traveling a lot, I played many tournaments. Today I’m here, I’m very happy to fight for this crown, and I’ll try to enjoy the match. I know it will be very hard, it’s my first experience, and we’ll see. But anyway, I’m happy—many chess players play their whole life in chess and they don’t have a chance to play for this, so I’m happy that today I have a chance to fight for this.
Many chess players play their whole life in chess and they don't have a chance to play for this.
Javokhir Sindarov has a chance of a lifetime. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.
What do you expect from Gukesh?

Sindarov: Gukesh’s performance in 2024 is something fantastic and we already know he played very well. Of course, if you took his last year, he’s unlucky, but still, this year I played against him in Tata Steel, and I feel he’s really very strong. Sometimes you have bad periods, but I think it doesn’t mean a lot, because like we saw with Ding also in 2024, he played very bad tournaments, but still in the match he played well. I don’t think we need to think about all of this stuff. I’m just trying to play against a strong opponent and trying to enjoy the match.
Is the role of defending a title more difficult?
Gukesh: I don’t think I’m here to defend anything—I’m here to win it all over again! That’s the mindset I’m in.
I don’t think I’m here to defend anything—I’m here to win it all over again!
Gukesh has had a tough couple of years, but was in fine form in the press conference. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.
How do you rate your chances?

Sindarov: I’ve had many interviews about this, but I think I’ll say the chances are 50:50. I don’t want to say anything, because the match will be very tough. It’s normal to give 50:50, because it’s a hard match, 14 games, and anything can happen.
What will the players eat during the match?

Gukesh: I generally prefer just food that I’m comfortable with. Usually I eat a lot of Indian food. Some people in Geneva have been very kind to prepare food for me, so I’m getting home-cooked Indian food, which I’m very comfortable with. So I’m very grateful for it.

Sindarov: Actually I’m the guy who can eat any cuisine, it doesn’t matter, but here I’m happy. In Samarkand our team had a special chef who made for us every day food. Our government was also bringing some chefs from Uzbekistan, but as I said, I’m really happy to have any food, and if I want to go after Sunday to some Japanese cuisine I’m really happy to go, so for me especially it doesn’t really matter a lot. I’m happy with everything.
Why did Sindarov play so much before the match, and did it surprise Gukesh?

Sindarov: We talked about this a little bit with Roman [Vidonyak, his coach]. First, I had an invitation from the Grand Chess Tour before I won the Candidates, and of course when you get to play such a strong tournament, when you have the opportunity, I immediately agreed to play. My goal even after I won the Candidates was to have more experience, because I didn’t play that many strong tournaments in my career. From this year probably I really start playing such strong tournaments as Tata Steel, so that’s why I chose to play many tournaments, and I’m happy with my decision.
I didn't play that many strong tournaments in my career.

Gukesh: Not really. Me and my team kind of expected that he’ll play more than me. We had decided to slow down the tournaments quite a bit this year, but basically the same reason that Sindarov has said, that this is kind of the first year that he’s been playing at the very elite, and we just thought that it made sense that he’ll make use of the good momentum and he’ll get more experience against the top guys. It was not a surprise at all.
What were the players looking for when inspecting the library playing hall?

Gukesh: I checked the playing hall yesterday. It was basically checking whether I’ll be able to feel comfortable for four-five hours every day. I checked the chairs, the lighting, the floors, different kinds of things that can bother you during a game. But I was happy with pretty much everything, and about the books—I just saw there were a lot of books, I didn’t really bother to check what books they are. I don’t think I’ll be reading in between the games!

Sindarov: It’s my first time that there’s nobody playing around us, only us. It can be boring sometimes, because you don’t know who to watch, because even in some other tournaments when I played, there should be someone who I always watch, but in general we looked at the rooms, everything. The playing hall is really very beautiful. I was thinking I’ll play in a box, but still it looks very fine, and I hope for a great match.
How was Sindarov’s training camp in October in Cyprus?

Sindarov: It was a great memory, I came back after the Candidates for the Cap St Georges Hotel and I want to say my thanks for the managers of the hotel. We had a great camp there. Somehow I met Hikaru there also, he was also taking a rest, he said he’s preparing for Clutch Chess, but in general I have a very good rest there and good preparation and our team was happy, so I’m really happy and maybe soon I’ll come back to this place.

While I'm not, I am advising him in a limited capacity about 2.Ke2. The OG prep was for an eventual WC match against Magnus, but as that won't be happening, the world deserves to have this prep in the open, so I'm sharing it. I've also heard that Magnus is sharing his 2.Ke2 prep with @DGukesh. Good Luck to Sindarov and Gukesh, may the best 2.Ke2 win!
Can the players reveal their seconds?
Gukesh: I’m here with Gaju, and other team members I would like to reveal later.
Sindarov: In my team here there’s Roman, and everybody knows Mukhiddin Madaminov is also here, and also Nikita Vitiugov is helping me here. I have other teams, but maybe after the match I will show.
Sindarov's team in Geneva wasn't hiding, with GM Shamsiddin Vokhidov one player Sindarov didn't name in the press conference. Photo: Y. E. Nisenbaum/FIDE.
What changes has AI made in chess?

Sindarov: In my opinion in the last six years the engines have changed a lot. Sometimes it’s become boring to prep such long lines, because before engines were showing some lines are very bad, but now it’s completely different evaluation there. In my opinion, chess became stronger. In general, openings mean a lot, but still you have to play very good chess, but I will say from other matches 10 years ago that opening preparation has changed really a lot. That’s the main point right now.
Gukesh's arrival at the Palace of Nations. Photo: Y. E. Nisenbaum.

Gukesh: I guess the clear answer is that opening prep has become much more computer-based and it’s very hard to disagree with the computers sometimes, but also, for example, the general level keeps rising the more people work with computers. They also learn a lot more ideas, not just opening ideas, but in general, they understand structures better, defense gets better, because the computer is always very resourceful. I think just working with computers has increased the level of chess by humans and made it much harder to win games, but also I think it makes it more of a sport. Everybody has access to similar things that help them like engines, seconds, coaches, but you need to find something that will help you be slightly better than the rest, which is what sport is about, I think.
I think it makes it more of a sport.
—Gukesh Dommaraju on the equalizing effect of AI in chess
How different is preparing for a single opponent?

Sindarov: The most different part of preparation, for Swiss tournaments, for small mini-matches, for a big match, it’s the opening. You need to work really a lot. I was thinking six months—I have enough time—but maybe even this six months, I played many tournaments, but still it’s also maybe not enough to prepare for such a hard tournament. It’s my first time and I’m starting to understand that when someone said for me it takes three-four months for prep for a world championship match I never believed that it can be normal, but now I understand how preparation is going. It was really hard, but exciting. I’m enjoying our training.
Have the players made any bets or promises for what they’ll do if they win, like Gukesh bungee jumping in 2024?

Sindarov: I think I have the same question in interviews, ‘What you will do?’ but really I don’t think about this, I don’t have any bets, because I tried many things in life. I have no idea what I will do, but I want to really focus and not think about this. The first thing I really want to do is focus on my next 20 days and try to play the best chess, and then we’ll see.
Gukesh: I’ve a couple of things in mind. I’ll do them! I think you’ll get to know in time, maybe.
Have they been to Switzerland before and what are their rest-day plans?

Gukesh: This is like my third or fourth time. I’ve played a few tournaments here, I also went on a little vacation to Interlaken, and that was pretty nice also. I don’t have any plans for the rest day, but just the hotel we’re staying in is quite nice, just in front of the lake. Maybe after the tournament I’ll do something.

Sindarov: The first time in 2024 I went to many places here, mostly I loved Lauterbrunnen, it’s fantastic, really, especially in summer. I recommended for my family also this place. My coach Roman lives in Munich, it’s very close to Switzerland, and we come here by car, and he has a lot of students here and I met with a lot of his students, and it’s my third time. I’ve never been in Geneva, Geneva is very beautiful, I like the lake, everything here. The weather is also very good right now. I was thinking it would be more cold, but somehow it’s very good weather and I’m enjoying the city. For the rest day, probably I will play more video games!
What did the players have to give up as children to be so good now?

Sindarov: All my life, I never worked seriously until 2025. I know that I always had a great talent in chess, not in chess, maybe in every game, because I have something that if I play some games I always try to win. It was in any game. When I started working on chess, I became stronger, so I recommend to everyone, to work on anything you like. If you love to play football, work on football, because I think with hard work everything will also come. The last two years I worked a lot and I won a lot of tournaments. Also I was lucky to do it, but still I worked a lot, so I recommend to all children everywhere, in any sport, work a lot on yourself. That means a lot, in my opinion.
Things came easily to Javokhir Sindarov. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

Gukesh: The things I gave were probably a lot of time for different things in childhood—I didn’t really go to school, or anything like that. But also, I’m grateful for this kind of life that not many people get to live, and surely many people wouldn’t mind, so I’m grateful for it. There are some things that maybe I did miss, but it always felt worth it, and now through chess I also developed a lot of other interests that I make time for these days. I don’t really feel like I would have it any other way!
I'm grateful for this kind of life that not many people get to live.
How did they prepare mentally and physically?

Gukesh: Physically I in general play a lot of different sports. I was also surfing quite a bit. Some mild workouts, but mostly I just stayed active, outdoor sports like running. Mentally, I’m continuing to work with my sports psychologist Paddy [Upton], that has also been going great, he has been very helpful since the time we started working together, and other than that, I read from time to time about different kinds of stuff. The usual stuff. Nothing special.

Sindarov: Physically I also love to play many sports. In Cyprus I started playing and loving padel. I have played a lot in my camps also. I think you also have to do some physical things. Also I’m young, for such a hard match. If I would be 30, 40 then maybe it would be tough, but because I’m young, I think it will not be very hard physically, but mentally I think it’s important and I work on that with my coaches. Everything is fine!
The opening ceremony beneath the shield of the United Nations. Photo: Y. E. Nisenbaum/FIDE.

Sindarov: You know my character, I always try to win, but we played a lot in Samarkand, me and my grandfather against both Nodirbeks, and sometimes it was our day, sometimes their day, so basically I think we finished in the end with the same result.
Is it harder or easier this time for Gukesh?

Gukesh: The preparation differs from match to match. I think in ’24 I was also playing a lot more than I did this year. It depends, sometimes it just feels like hard work when you do certain kinds of work, sometimes it just feels so much like fun, and creativity flowing around. Also I think just working with a team that I enjoy being around is one of the most important things for me, so that even when the work is exhausting or stressful you’re still surrounded by people who you like being around, and that gives you a lot of strength. In that sense, actually, I feel the best part of this whole world championship journey is the training camps, it’s so much fun, so much good work with so much laughing, so many jokes. With Gaju I share a very close personal bond. The training camps are probably the things I will most remember after the match.
I feel the best part of this whole world championship journey is the training camps.
What useful piece of advice did they get from friends, family, or mentors?

Gukesh: I think I’ve gotten a lot of advice from my team, my friends, my family. Probably the ones that stick the most with me are in difficult moments when someone says, “Just go there and express yourself, it doesn’t matter whatever happens, we are there for you!” and also one thing that in the last few months has stuck with me is somebody said, “Remember who you are!” And I think in this match I will remember that.

Sindarov: I don’t have anything that I always take for every moment of my life, but during hard periods I think it’s important my friends, my family always support me during tournaments, if I have some problems. That’s why I really say my big thanks to them, because in every hard moment in my life they always give the first hand to help me, and I think it’s very hard to have such strong results if you don’t have good friends and family in front of you, so I think it’s very important.
I think it's very hard to have such strong results if you don't have good friends and family in front of you.
How well do they know each other’s games?

Sindarov: We haven’t played too many games against each other, but I learn from his games also a lot. I will say he has very good strengths in some typical positions, his calculation is very good. I also really like that Gukesh can fight until the end. I remember how he pushed against Wei Yi in a very important game in the Olympiad 2024. It’s really a very good strength in chess in my opinion.
The trophy the players are competing for. Photo: Y. E. Nisenbaum/FIDE.

Gukesh: When you play a world championship it’s very nice that it’s just one opponent so you can put full attention on that one specific player and yeah, there’s a lot of analyzing your opponent going on. I think also it’s only to an extent, because most of the guys, especially Sindarov, are very much universal. He can play any position at a decent level, and it’s just you sharpening your skills, understanding your opponent to a good degree, and I don’t think there’s more than that.
The players now have a day to rest before the action starts on Tuesday, with the whole chess world watching!
